span.label: WHAT A STATISTIC MEANS WHEN THE MODEL GETS COMPLICATED - R-squared and the intra-class correlation for generalized linear mixed models, revisited by the authors of the previous definition and extended to families their own method could not reach
span.quote: The coefficient of determination R 2 quantifies the proportion of variance explained by a statistical model and is an important summary statistic of biological interest. However, estimating R 2 for generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) remains challenging.

span.label: how to define the residual variance term that R-squared needs, when for most distributional families it CANNOT BE SEPARATED into the components the earlier definition assumed
span.quote: However, obtaining for specific distributions is not always possible, because in many families of GLMMs, (observation-level variance) cannot be clearly separated into (overdispersion variance) and (distribution-specific variance). It turns out that binomial and Poisson distributions are special cases where can be usefully calculated, because either all overdispersion is modelled by an OLRE (additive overdispersion) or by a single multiplicative overdispersion parameter (multiplicative overdispersion). This is not the case for other families.

span.label: a general definition of the observation-level variance for non-Gaussian GLMMs via the delta method, the lognormal approximation or the trigamma function - plus a correction to two of their own earlier recommendations
span.quote: As shown in the electronic supplementary material, appendix S2, ln(1 + 1/ λ ) (lognormal approximation), 1/ λ (delta method approximation) and (trigamma function) give similar results when λ is greater than 2. Our recommendation is to use the trigamma function for obtaining whenever this is possible.

span.label: **A NAMING RULE - WHEN A MODIFIER IN A NAME IS LICENSED**: `In such a case, THE ICC SHOULD NOT BE CALLED `ADJUSTED`. FOR AN ICC VALUE TO BE ADJUSTED FOR A SOURCE OF VARIANCE, THAT VARIANCE MUST BE MORE THAN 0 AND OMITTED FROM THE ICC CALCULATION.` A published condition on the use of one word inside a statistic's name - the same shape as buck2011's rule for when two fields may share an acronym, one level down
span.quote: In such a case, the ICC should not be called ‘adjusted’ ( sensu [ 2 ]). For an ICC value to be adjusted for a source of variance, that variance must be more than 0 and omitted from the ICC calculation.

span.label: AND ONE NAME FOR TWO QUANTITIES, KEPT APART BY A SUBSCRIPT: `MARGINAL AND CONDITIONAL R2 DIFFER ONLY IN WHETHER THE RANDOM EFFECT VARIANCE IS INCLUDED IN THE NUMERATOR` - the marginal is the proportion explained by the fixed effects, the conditional by fixed AND random. Two numbers a reader will see reported as `R2`
span.quote: where represents the marginal R 2 , which is the proportion of the total variance explained by the fixed effects, represents the conditional R 2 , which is the proportion of the variance explained by both fixed and random effects, and is the variance explained by fixed effects [ 11 ]. As marginal and conditional R 2 differ only in whether the random effect variance is included in the numerator, we avoid redundancy and present equations only for marginal R 2 in the following.

span.label: **AND A RENAMING WHERE THE NOTATION DELIBERATELY DOES NOT FOLLOW**: `We refer to this generalized version ... as `THE OBSERVATION-LEVEL VARIANCE` HERE RATHER THAN THE RESIDUAL VARIANCE (BUT WE KEEP THE NOTATION). Note that the observation-level variance SHOULD NOT BE CONFUSED WITH the variance associated with OLRE, which ... can be considered to be A PART OF it.` The name changes, the symbol does not, and the sentence that renames it also warns which neighbouring term it is not
span.quote: However, as we will show below, we can always obtain the GLMM version of (on the latent scale) directly. We refer to this generalized version of as ‘the observation-level variance’ here rather than the residual variance (but we keep the notation ). Note that the observation-level variance, , should not be confused with the variance associated with OLRE, which estimates and can be considered to be a part of .

span.label: AND THE EARLIER DEFINITION WORKED ONLY FOR TWO SPECIAL CASES, SAID PLAINLY: `obtaining for specific distributions IS NOT ALWAYS POSSIBLE, because IN MANY FAMILIES OF GLMMs, (observation-level variance) CANNOT BE CLEARLY SEPARATED INTO (overdispersion variance) AND (distribution-specific variance). IT TURNS OUT THAT BINOMIAL AND POISSON DISTRIBUTIONS ARE SPECIAL CASES where can be usefully calculated ... THIS IS NOT THE CASE FOR OTHER FAMILIES.` The general method was a special case and the authors are the ones who found out
span.quote: However, obtaining for specific distributions is not always possible, because in many families of GLMMs, (observation-level variance) cannot be clearly separated into (overdispersion variance) and (distribution-specific variance). It turns out that binomial and Poisson distributions are special cases where can be usefully calculated, because either all overdispersion is modelled by an OLRE (additive overdispersion) or by a single multiplicative overdispersion parameter (multiplicative overdispersion). This is not the case for other families.

span.label: AND A DISTINCTION THE AUTHORS WITHDRAW FOR ONE FAMILY AND KEEP FOR ANOTHER: `IN THE PAST, WE DISTINGUISHED BETWEEN ICC ON THE LATENT SCALE AND ON THE OBSERVATION SCALE. SUCH A DISTINCTION TURNS OUT TO BE STRICTLY APPROPRIATE ONLY FOR BINOMIAL DISTRIBUTIONS BUT NOT FOR POISSON DISTRIBUTIONS (AND PROBABLY ALSO NOT FOR OTHER NON-GAUSSIAN DISTRIBUTIONS).` A retraction with its scope stated, including the part they are only probably right about
span.quote: In the past, we distinguished between ICC on the latent scale and on the observation scale [ 2 ]. Such a distinction turns out to be strictly appropriate only for binomial distributions but not for Poisson distributions (and probably also not for other non-Gaussian distributions). This is because the property of what we have called the distribution-specific variance for binomial distributions (e.g. π 2 /3 for binomial error distribution with the logit-link function) is quite different from what we have discussed as the observation-level variance although these two types of variance are related conceptually

span.label: AND THEY NAME WHAT THEY USED TO CALL IT: `note that WE WOULD HAVE CALLED 1/lambda THE DISTRIBUTION-SPECIFIC VARIANCE` - the same quantity, the old name, and the new one, in a parenthesis. **The corpus has papers that rename things and papers that correct things; this one prints the substitution table**
span.quote: As with the observation-level variance for the log-Poisson model (which is 1/ λ and changes with λ ; note that we would have called 1/ λ the distribution-specific variance; [ 2 , 3 ]), the observation-level variance of the binomial distribution changes as p changes (see electronic supplementary material, appendix S5), suggesting these two observation-level variances (1/ λ and 1/( np (1 – p )) are analogous while the distribution-specific variance

span.label: **AND THE NAMING CHOICE MOVES EVERY REPORTED NUMBER, IN A KNOWN DIRECTION**: `the MINIMUM VALUE of 1/(p(1-p)) IS 4, WHICH IS LARGER THAN pi^2/3 = 3.29, MEANING THAT THE USE OF 1/p(1-p) IN R2 AND ICC FOR BINARY DATA WILL ALWAYS PRODUCE LARGER VALUES THAN THOSE USING pi^2/3.` Which term you call the denominator decides whether every R2 in a literature is larger or smaller - not a range, a DIRECTION, with a floor. And Browne et al. observed exactly that
span.quote: Further, the minimum value of 1/( p (1 – p )) is 4, which is larger than π 2 /3 ≈ 3.29, meaning that the use of 1/ p (1 – p ) in R 2 and ICC for binary data will always produce larger values than those using π 2 /3. Consequently, Browne et al . [ 14 ] showed that ICC values (or variance partition coefficients, VPCs) estimated using π 2 /3 were higher than corresponding ICC values on the observation (original) scale using logistic-binomial GLMMs

span.label: AND TWO OF THEIR OWN EARLIER RECOMMENDATIONS CONTRADICT EACH OTHER: `In our earlier papers, WE PROPOSED TO USE THE EXPONENTIAL OF THE INTERCEPT ... WE ALSO SUGGESTED that it is possible to USE THE MEAN OF OBSERVED VALUES. UNFORTUNATELY, THESE TWO RECOMMENDATIONS ARE OFTEN INCONSISTENT WITH EACH OTHER.` Two ways to compute one input, from one paper, that disagree
span.quote: In our earlier papers, we proposed to use the exponential of the intercept, exp( β 0 ) (from the intercept-only model) as an estimator of λ [ 2 , 3 ]; note that exp( β 0 ) from models with any fixed effects will often be different from exp( β 0 ) from the intercept-only model. We also suggested that it is possible to use the mean of observed values y ij . Unfortunately, these two recommendations are often inconsistent with each other.

span.label: AND THE REASON IS THAT ONE OF THEM ESTIMATES A DIFFERENT LOCATION ENTIRELY: `In fact, exp(beta0) GIVES THE MEDIAN VALUE of y RATHER THAN THE MEAN ... Thus, the use of exp(beta0) will often OVERESTIMATE, providing SMALLER ESTIMATES OF R2 AND ICC ... when lambda is small, THE DIFFERENCE CAN BE SUBSTANTIAL SO THE CHOICE OF THE METHOD NEEDS TO BE REPORTED FOR REPRODUCIBILITY.` A methods choice promoted to a reporting requirement because the two answers differ
span.quote: In fact, exp( β 0 ) gives the median value of y ij rather than the mean of y ij , assuming a Poisson distribution. Thus, the use of exp( β 0 ) will often overestimate , providing smaller estimates of R 2 and ICC, compared to when using averaged y ij (which is usually a better estimate of E [ y ij ]). Quantitative differences between the two approaches may often be negligible, but when λ is small, the difference can be substantial so the choice of the method needs to be reported for reproducibility

span.label: AND THREE ROUTES REACH ONE QUANTITY AND AGREE ONLY ABOVE A THRESHOLD: `ln(1 + 1/lambda) (LOGNORMAL APPROXIMATION), 1/lambda (DELTA METHOD APPROXIMATION) and (TRIGAMMA FUNCTION) GIVE SIMILAR RESULTS WHEN LAMBDA IS GREATER THAN 2. OUR RECOMMENDATION IS TO USE THE TRIGAMMA FUNCTION.` Three names, one target, and a condition under which the choice stops mattering
span.quote: As shown in the electronic supplementary material, appendix S2, ln(1 + 1/ λ ) (lognormal approximation), 1/ λ (delta method approximation) and (trigamma function) give similar results when λ is greater than 2. Our recommendation is to use the trigamma function for obtaining whenever this is possible.

span.label: THEIR OWN APPROXIMATION IS NOT THE BEST ONE, AND THEY SAY SO: `A comparison among equations (6.7)-(6.9) is also shown in electronic supplementary material, appendix S3 (IT TURNS OUT EQUATION (6.8) GIVES THE BEST APPROXIMATION). SIMULATION WILL GIVE THE MOST ACCURATE CONVERSIONS when no exact solutions are available.` Equation 6.7 is theirs; 6.8 is McCulloch et al.'s
span.quote: A comparison among equations (6.7)–(6.9) is also shown in electronic supplementary material, appendix S3 (it turns out equation (6.8) gives the best approximation). Simulation will give the most accurate conversions when no exact solutions are available.

span.label: AND A NEIGHBOURING STATISTIC IS ADMITTED INTO THE FAMILY WITH A HEDGE IN PARENTHESES: the trigamma function has been used for `HERITABILITY (WHICH CAN BE SEEN AS A TYPE OF ICC ALTHOUGH IN A STRICT SENSE, IT IS NOT)`. A kindhood claim and its denial in eleven words - the corpus's `is-a` cannot carry that, so it is here in prose
span.quote: The trigamma function has been previously used to obtain observation-level variance in calculations of heritability (which can be seen as a type of ICC although in a strict sense, it is not; see [ 25 ]) using negative binomial GLMMs

span.label: and one field renames the statistic outright: `a TYPE OF ICC IS OFTEN REFERRED TO AS REPEATABILITY R, where the grouping factor is often individuals that have been phenotyped repeatedly` - ecology and evolution's name for what the rest of the literature calls an intra-class correlation
span.quote: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) is a related statistic that quantifies the proportion of variance explained by a grouping (random) factor in multilevel/hierarchical data. In the field of ecology and evolution, a type of ICC is often referred to as repeatability R , where the grouping factor is often individuals that have been phenotyped repeatedly

span.term: adjusted ICC (the condition on the word)
span.quote: In such a case, the ICC should not be called ‘adjusted’ ( sensu [ 2 ]). For an ICC value to be adjusted for a source of variance, that variance must be more than 0 and omitted from the ICC calculation.

span.quote: Further, the minimum value of 1/( p (1 – p )) is 4, which is larger than π 2 /3 ≈ 3.29, meaning that the use of 1/ p (1 – p ) in R 2 and ICC for binary data will always produce larger values than those using π 2 /3. Consequently, Browne et al . span.label: the proportion of variance explained by a grouping factor - called `REPEATABILITY R` in ecology and evolution, and a statistic whose `adjusted` variant carries a published condition on the word
span.quote: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) is a related statistic that quantifies the proportion of variance explained by a grouping (random) factor in multilevel/hierarchical data. In the field of ecology and evolution, a type of ICC is often referred to as repeatability R , where the grouping factor is often individuals that have been phenotyped repeatedly

span.quote: However, obtaining for specific distributions is not always possible, because in many families of GLMMs, (observation-level variance) cannot be clearly separated into (overdispersion variance) and (distribution-specific variance). It turns out that binomial and Poisson distributions are special cases where can be usefully calculated, because either all overdispersion is modelled by an OLRE (additive overdispersion) or by a single multiplicative overdispersion parameter (multiplicative overdispersion).
